title: How to use SUMIF in Excel
description: Learn how to use SUMIF in Excel to add cells based on a condition. See formula examples, syntax, common mistakes, and try hands-on practice.

args.name: range
args.text: The range of cells you want evaluated by your condition.

args.name: criteria
args.text: The condition that determines which cells to add, such as ">50", 10, or "Bread".

args.name: sum_range
args.text: The actual cells to add if different from range. If omitted, Excel sums the cells in range.

sections.heading: What SUMIF does
sections.text: **SUMIF** adds values in a range that meet one condition you specify. You can test numbers against a threshold or check text in one column and add matching amounts from another.

sections.heading: Sum values that meet a condition
sections.text: When your condition and the values to add are in the same column, pass two arguments: the range and the criteria. Enclose comparison operators in quotation marks. Here, the formula adds all sales amounts greater than 50.

sections.heading: Sum matching values from another column
sections.text: To check one column and add numbers from a different column, add `sum_range` as the third argument. The formula checks the category in column A and adds the box counts in column B for matching rows.

sections.heading: Common mistake: missing quotes around operators
sections.text: When your criteria uses comparison operators such as `>`, `<`, or `<>`, you must enclose both the operator and the number in quotation marks, like `">50"`. Writing `=SUMIF(B2:B5, >50)` without quotes causes a syntax error. To combine an operator with a cell reference such as `C1`, join them with an ampersand: `">"&C1`.
